Yet this consciousness is consciousness only of the phenomenon through cognition; cognition is cognition only of the phenomenon through consciousness; and the phenomenon is the appearance of reality to a consciousness through cognition.
So the phenomenologist considers this reality precisely in its character as appearance or phenomenon.
He describes the way a reality appears to itself through cognition to a consciousness, and therefore appears as a phenomenon.
But once he has described this phenomenon, the phenomenologist naturally asks what this reality is that “makes itself appear” in this way to a consciousness through cognition.
He asks what this cognition is through which reality appears in this way to consciousness.
And he asks what this consciousness is to which reality appears in this way through cognition.
In other words, he searches for the cause of the phenomenon.
And he finds it in the human being in the world studied by the cosmologist.

But once he begins speaking about the human being who, through cognition and within consciousness, makes both the world and himself appear, and about the world that appears through humanity, the phenomenologist ceases to be merely a phenomenologist.
He becomes a cosmologist—that is, a philosopher.

Phenomenology therefore presents itself from the outset as a philosophical science. For that reason, it has nothing to do with what we ordinarily call “science.” In particular, it differs fundamentally and radically from scientific psychology and scientific history.

As a philosophical science, Phenomenology is not “abstract” but “concrete.” When the phenomenologist studies an “object,” he does not set aside the questions of how and through what means that object is given to him, or who he himself is—in other words, who this person is to whom the object is given in this particular way.

Taken as a whole, then, the text of the Phenomenology—its entire subject matter—does more than give a complete description of its “object.” It also explains how its own particular way of knowing that object is possible, and it answers the question of who its author is: who is this phenomenological “consciousness” to which a phenomenological object becomes “given” through a phenomenological form of cognition?

More simply, Phenomenology includes within its description of what it describes an account of how it describes it and of who is doing the describing. Alongside its object, its subject matter therefore includes both itself and its author.

Ordinary “science,” by contrast—and psychology and history in particular—limits itself to describing its “objects.” Its subject matter coincides with its object, or more exactly, consists only in a description of that object. The question of how the object is given, and to whom, lies outside the field of inquiry.

Yet an object must in fact be given to some particular person in some particular way if it is ever to become the subject of a description. “Science” forgets this and therefore imagines that it is describing the “object” simply as it exists “in reality.”
But precisely because it thinks this way, while forgetting that the object is given in a particular way to a particular person, science actually describes only how that object appears to it.

Science thinks it is dealing with “reality itself”—in effect, mistakenly taking itself for a kind of Cosmology. But what it actually deals with are “phenomena,” and these are what it describes. A “phenomenon,” however—and the unconscious, scientific description of it—is determined not only by the object that appears, but also by the way it appears and by the person to whom it appears.

A particular science therefore describes, on the one hand, only a particular aspect of its object: specifically, the aspect revealed by the particular form of cognition characteristic of that science. On the other hand, it describes only the aspect given to a particular observer—to the consciousness of the person who created that science.

And this consciousness is determined not only by what is given to it, but also by the kind of human being who embodies it—that is, by that person’s individual interests and class interests. In this sense, “science” itself appears as a social ideology: a class opinion, rather than knowledge in the full sense of the word.
So “science,” without realizing it, describes isolated ideological aspects of reality—or of the cosmos, meaning the world in the broadest sense.

Phenomenology is different. Because it takes account both of how reality is given and of the person to whom it is given, it deals, in principle, with reality itself rather than with isolated ideological aspects of reality.

As the development of Phenomenology will show, its object is not given to it through one isolated form of cognition. Phenomenology makes use of cognition as a whole—that is, of all possible forms of cognition taken together. It is therefore given not one isolated aspect of its object, but all its aspects: the object itself, viewed from every side.

And because Phenomenology also includes an account of its author’s consciousness—while showing that this consciousness is not confined by one particular set of historical conditions—it describes not merely what is given to this particular author, or to his class or nation according to private, class, or national interests. It describes what is given to consciousness as such.
Phenomenology therefore presents not an “ideology,” not a private, social, or national opinion, but knowledge in the strict sense: something that reveals reality itself.
In other words, Phenomenology differs from science because it actually achieves what science ultimately claims to achieve without being entitled to that claim.

Phenomenology is not an ideological opinion about some isolated aspect of an object. It is genuine knowledge of the object itself, taken as a whole. This is what makes Phenomenology a philosophical science, as distinct from every “science” in the ordinary sense—including psychology and history.

In its philosophical approach or point of view, Phenomenology does not differ from the other two philosophical sciences, Cosmology and Ontology, which together make up systematic Philosophy, or Philosophy in the narrow sense. Like them, Phenomenology is true knowledge of its object itself, taken as a whole.
What distinguishes Phenomenology from them is the nature of its object.
The object of Phenomenology is the totality of all possible “phenomena”: all the natural and human appearances of reality as it appears to human beings.

Cosmology, by contrast, studies “reality as it exists in itself,” whether natural or human, as the “cause” of these appearances. Ontology studies being itself, both real and ideal, which lies “beneath” existing reality and which “makes itself appear” to human beings.

The special nature of the phenomenological object therefore distinguishes Phenomenology not only from systematic Philosophy but also from ordinary “science,” whether natural science or the human sciences—psychology and history in the broad sense.
Consider nature first: the natural world.

A natural “science” such as physics mistakenly thinks that it is dealing with the world itself. In fact, only philosophical Cosmology deals with the natural world as such; indeed, the first part of Cosmology is devoted to it.
Science, for its part, describes the world as it appears to science, without realizing that what it is describing is precisely an appearing world.
Phenomenology consciously does something else. It does not describe the natural world as such. It describes the world’s appearance to human beings—the natural world as a phenomenon.

And if it describes the “phenomenon” of the natural world, it must speak not only about that world but also about how it appears and to whom it appears. It therefore describes not only the appearance or phenomenon of the natural world, but also the cognition through which the world appears and the consciousness to which it appears through that cognition.
But whose cognition is this, and whose consciousness?

Phenomenology is a philosophical science and therefore possesses true and complete knowledge of its object. If the natural world itself were its object, Phenomenology would possess true and complete knowledge of the natural world itself. But in that case it would not be Phenomenology at all. It would be Cosmology.

So the natural world whose “appearance” Phenomenology describes is not given to Phenomenology itself—not through phenomenological cognition, not to phenomenological consciousness, and therefore not to the author of a Phenomenology.
What is phenomenologically given to the phenomenologist is the appearance of the natural world, not the natural world itself.

Phenomenology does, of course, describe its own phenomenological knowledge of this appearance and the consciousness that possesses that knowledge. But this must not be confused with the consciousness and cognition to which the world itself appears.

We can put the distinction this way. The “appearance of the world” described by Phenomenology does not itself “appear” to phenomenological consciousness through phenomenological cognition. Rather, it is phenomenologically given to phenomenological knowledge through that knowledge itself.
It is the natural world that “appears” to a non-phenomenological consciousness, through a non-phenomenological form of cognition.
So to whom does the world appear, and how?
Clearly, it appears to human consciousness, through a human way of knowing. And we have already seen that this consciousness and cognition cannot themselves be phenomenological or philosophical.

The natural world therefore “appears” to the consciousness of any non-phenomenologist or non-philosopher who knows it in some way: to an ordinary person “in love with nature,” for example, or to a scientist studying nature, such as a physicist, and so on.
Unlike Cosmology, then, Phenomenology does not describe the natural world itself. And unlike the scientist or layperson, it does not mistakenly imagine that it is doing so.

Instead, it consciously describes how the natural world appears to a particular consciousness—whether that of an ordinary person, a physicist, or someone else—through sensory perception, physical science, or some other form of cognition.

And it also describes how this appearance of the world is given to a non-phenomenological consciousness through non-phenomenological cognition; how that consciousness and cognition are in turn given to the phenomenologist’s knowledge; and how phenomenological knowledge itself, together with the phenomenologist who possesses it, is also given within that same knowledge.
Phenomenology therefore differs from natural science in its object. It studies not nature itself but nature as it appears to human beings.
Phenomenology is consequently not a science of nature, but a science of human beings—human beings to whom, among other things, the natural world appears.

Because Phenomenology leaves nature itself aside, it cannot tell us how true what human beings say about nature actually is—that is, how closely their account corresponds to reality. From Phenomenology we do not learn what nature is. We learn only what human beings are, insofar as one of their defining features is that they come to know the natural world in particular ways.
So, as we have already said, Phenomenology is ultimately a kind of anthropology: a science of human beings.
And since anthropology can be divided into psychology and history, in the broad sense of both terms, Phenomenology can also be called both psychology and history.

Yet although Phenomenology is indeed a science of human beings rather than of nature, it is still not a “science” of human beings in the ordinary sense. It is not the same thing as conventional psychology or conventional history.
As phenomenological, or philosophical, anthropology, it differs from both scientific psychology and scientific history.
We can now ask exactly what this means.

Phenomenology differs from psychology and history because Philosophy, in the broad sense, differs from “science” in two ways. Its approach is different: unlike the psychologist or historian, the phenomenologist includes himself within the investigation of his own object. But the object itself is also different.

We have just seen that, because Phenomenology does not deal with the natural world itself, it speaks not about the world as such but about the appearance of the world to human beings. In the end, then, it speaks about human beings—or more precisely, about human consciousness and human cognition of the world.
But consciousness and cognition are precisely what psychology studies.

Even so, Phenomenology also speaks about the world’s appearance itself—about the world insofar as it appears to human beings. It therefore speaks not only about consciousness and cognition, but also about the content of cognition.
And in this respect its object differs fundamentally from the object of psychology.

Suppose psychology wants to study a person’s consciousness and the sensory cognition contained in it—for example, the perception of a birch tree. Psychology does not, however, describe the birch tree as sensibly known.

Phenomenology, by contrast, is therefore as much a “history of natural science” as it is a psychology of natural science. It describes all the different ways in which the natural world can appear to human beings: what it “seems” to be to the layperson, the scientist, and others under different historical conditions.

In our terminology, psychology studies not cognition together with the consciousness that possesses it, but cognition taken on its own. It does not describe the human being who possesses the cognition it studies.
Psychology therefore loses sight of the fact that cognition itself is conditioned by the historical—especially social and political—conditions of human life.
And everything we have just said remains true when the object of human cognition is no longer the natural world but human beings themselves and the historical world they have created.

Psychology abstracts so completely from the “phenomenon” itself—from the “content of consciousness,” or more exactly from the content of cognition—that the very distinction between knowing the natural world and knowing the human world becomes irrelevant to it. Psychology speaks about cognition in general, regardless of what is being known.
Phenomenology does the opposite. It describes not only cognition but its content, including the human world insofar as that world “appears” to human consciousness through cognition.
It describes not only human cognition of the world and of humanity, but the world and humanity themselves insofar as they appear to human beings.
And because human beings also “appear” to the psychologist, Phenomenology will describe the psychologist’s consciousness as psychologist and the psychologist’s cognition—that is, psychology itself.

The objects of psychology and Phenomenology therefore differ so radically that psychology itself becomes an object—or more precisely, one of the objects—of Phenomenology, while psychology as such scarcely suspects that Phenomenology exists, or even that human cognition can be studied phenomenologically rather than psychologically.

To put it differently: unlike Cosmology, which really does study cognition itself as part of reality, and unlike psychology, which merely claims to do so, Phenomenology studies the appearance of cognition to human beings—more exactly, to non-philosophers or non-phenomenologists, including the psychologist.
It therefore describes not only what cognition “seems to be” to different non-phenomenologists under different historical conditions, but also how and why it seems that way to them.
And finally, it describes the people to whom it seems that way, insofar as it seems that way to them.

So when Phenomenology discusses “psychological laws,” for example, it does not merely describe those laws as a particular way in which cognition appears to human beings. It also investigates how psychology comes to know those laws and who this psychologist is—or more exactly, what kind of “psychological consciousness” discovers them.
By excluding the content of the cognition it studies and excluding the consciousness that possesses that cognition, psychology necessarily becomes profoundly unhistorical.

As we will see, the driving force of historical development is not the “abstract” cognition or consciousness described by psychologists. It is the concrete human being, acting through work and struggle.
The psychologist’s “consciousness in general” obviously cannot work or struggle.

Psychology as such is therefore completely incapable of explaining how history can exist. For this reason, it tends in effect to deny history by treating the consciousness it studies as “eternal and unchanging,” even as independent of historical conditions—social, political, technical, and economic.
In one sense, psychology is right.
The abstract consciousness it studies really is “eternal and unchanging.” If one likes, one can say that consciousness itself does not change; only its content does.

Sensory perception and reason, considered simply as such, are the same in the ordinary person and the scientist, in a Stone Age human being and a medieval Christian, in an Australian “savage” and a contemporary French person.

Only differences in content, whether sensory or rational, allow us to distinguish the “consciousness of the layperson” from that of the “scientist,” the consciousness of the “primitive” from that of the “medieval person,” or the consciousness of the “bourgeois” from that of the “proletarian.”
Because psychology abstracts from the content of consciousness, it deals with abstractions—with a kind of consciousness that has never actually existed anywhere.

It therefore fails to notice that concrete consciousness, which is what Phenomenology studies, is necessarily the consciousness of a particular historical form of life: “primitive,” “medieval,” “proletarian,” and so on.
In this sense, as we have already seen, Phenomenology can also be said to differ from scientific psychology through its historical character.
But Phenomenology is historical only because its object is historical.

And its object is historical because it is not an abstract “consciousness.” It consists of an appearance or phenomenon—the content of a cognition or consciousness—plus the cognition through which that aspect of reality appears, plus the consciousness that possesses that cognition.
The structure of its object therefore makes Phenomenology historical and distinguishes it from psychology.
Yet precisely the same structure also distinguishes Phenomenology from history.
So if we call Phenomenology a kind of “historical psychology,” this is only to distinguish it from traditional scientific psychology, not to bring it closer to ordinary scientific history.
Its object is just as far removed from the object of scientific history as it is from that of scientific psychology.
To emphasize this other difference, we could equally well call it a kind of “psychological history.”
Using our terminology, we can say that psychology ordinarily forgets both the “phenomenon” and the “consciousness” when it speaks about “cognition”—or at least forgets the consciousness.
History does the opposite. When it speaks about the “phenomenon,” it usually forgets both the “cognition” and the “consciousness”—or at least the cognition.
